*"You probably think that your mom's meatballs are the best meatballs, just like I think my mom's meatballs are the best ones, but it could be that neither one makes the best meatballs" - a doctor conversation with each other in the hospital cafeteria*

If I am considered to be the best in someone's eyes, but someone else thinks that another person is the best, am I truly the best? Are we all someone's best/favorite only to realize that it means that none of us are the best.

My mother is feeling ill---she has been sick her whole life, a sickness that exhausts the body. It's genetic---this disease...but that is not what we are here for. The hospital lights are always blinding, the shuffling of staff and patients, the dull hum of the central unit---the ache building in my shoulders---I always carry my stress there.

My head hurts again, I've been here for over 9 hours. the stress will kill me, I've started to become numb again from the pain...I've become a sort of hospital ghost--floating around the hallways, standing still at times--the rain continued outside.

```         
it will pass   
            eventually
```
----------------------------------------

I would have been a good mother. I like to believe that this is true, and that if I had the chance to bring a child forth into the world, I would have the strength of my mother, the softness and patience of my sisters. But I stand here, childless—motherless, and worst of all, siblingless. I have not one connection on this Earth, not even that of a pet. 

*a draft I have of something I might write in the future. Interestingly enough, when I type "siblingless" it gives me a red underline: misspelled. It tells me to correct it as "sibling less" or "sibling-less", and while I can understand the clarity that the hyphen provides, I want the word itself to be difficult to read, an eyesore, because that is what I imagine being without my sibling.*

Books I've Read this Month:

- Água Viva by Clarice Lispector

Her most recognized work and I can say that it is absolutely beautiful. I actually started reading this book back at Wellesley, and it is pretty short, but it took me time to sit and process her thoughts. Her words flowed like a stream and I felt so many emotions while reading it; very difficult to explain, best to just read it yourself. 8.5/10

- The Year of Magical Thinking by Joan Didion

This book was gifted to me by my sister during my sophomore year. Now, everyone has this book, and I can understand why. Didion is a wonderful writer and what makes this book great is how raw she is with her emotions. This was a difficult read for me, simply because of how emotional I would get reading it. She not only writes about her pain and her grief but invites the reader to experience these stages with her. 10/10

- The Orange Eats Creeps by Grace Krilanovich

This book is weird, and yet so powerful. I originally was intrigued by the blurb which mentioned vampires and a girl trying to find her foster sister. I love a good book about sisterhood and I purchased it. I was not at all prepared for how raw, at times vulgar, and honest this book would be. It discusses drug use, prostitution and the vampires are not mythical creatures but humans that have fallen to using. No one likes to think about the people who live on the streets but their stories are real and important. The girl in the book was failed multiple times by society and the system but even while under the influence, her love and struggles to find her sister are real and heartbreaking. 8/10
